hints: Recall what power measures: work done per unit time, $P = W/t$, not work done itself.
Recall what work done by a constant force is: force $\times$ distance moved in the direction of the force.
Combine them as $P = Fd/t$ and ask what distance divided by time, $d/t$, represents for a moving object.
walkthrough: Start from the definition of power as the rate of transfer of energy: $P = W/t$, where $W$ is work done in $\text{J}$ and $t$ is time in $\text{s}$.
Recall the work done by a force acting along the displacement: $W = F \times d$, where $F$ is force in $\text{N}$ and $d$ is distance in $\text{m}$.
Substitute the work expression into the power expression: $P = (F \times d)/t = F \times (d/t)$.
Recognise that distance per unit time is speed in the direction of the force, and for directed motion this is velocity $v$ in $\text{m s}^{-1}$, so $P = F \times v$.

options.A: Force $\times$ distance is work done, $W = Fd$, measured in $\text{J}$, not the rate of doing work.
options.B: Power is the rate of working, $P = Fv$ for a force in the direction of velocity, with unit $\text{W}$.
options.C: Power is work done divided by time, $P = W/t$, so work done $\times$ time gives units $\text{J s}$ not power.
options.D: Work done $\times$ velocity gives units $\text{J m s}^{-1}$, which is not the watt $\text{W}$ for power.
